questions.q: What gap does an architecture decision record (ADR) fill that an ERD or sequence diagram doesn't?
options: It shows the exact field-level data model
It captures the reasoning behind a decision — why this option was chosen over the alternatives — not just the resulting structure or sequence
It replaces the need for any diagrams entirely
It shows the precise timing of API calls
questions.explain: Diagrams show the result of a decision (data shape, call order); an ADR captures the reasoning and rejected alternatives behind the decision itself, which no diagram records.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the five standard ADR sections described in this lesson?
options: Consequences — stating both the benefits and the costs the decision accepts
Lifeline
Cardinality
Activation bar
questions.explain: The standard ADR sections are Title, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences. Lifeline, cardinality, and activation bar are diagram-notation terms from earlier lessons, not ADR sections.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which ADR field is the one expected to change after the record is first written?
options: Context
Decision
Consequences
Status — e.g., moving from Proposed to Accepted, or later to Superseded
questions.explain: Status is the one field expected to change over time (Proposed → Accepted → possibly Deprecated or Superseded); the Context, Decision, and Consequences text of an accepted ADR is treated as immutable.

questions.q: If a team decides eighteen months later that an earlier ADR's decision was wrong, what does this lesson say is the correct fix?
options: Edit the original ADR's Decision section to reflect the new choice
Delete the original ADR so it no longer misleads readers
Write a new ADR recording the new decision, and mark the old ADR's status as superseded by the new one — leaving the old record's original text unchanged
Leave the Status field blank until the team is fully certain of the new direction
questions.explain: ADRs are treated as an immutable log: the fix for a reversed decision is a new ADR that supersedes the old one, with the old record's original content left exactly as it was written at the time.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which kind of decision 'earns its place' as an ADR?
options: Any decision at all, including trivial UI label wording, since every choice should be documented identically
A decision that is architecturally significant, genuinely debated among real alternatives, and likely to be questioned later
Only decisions that are later proven correct
Only decisions made by a Certified Technical Architect
questions.explain: An ADR is reserved for decisions that would be expensive or risky to reverse, had real alternatives on the table, and are the kind of choice a future reader would predictably ask 'why didn't we just do X' about.
